comparison: Both evaluate the implementation science component (C55-C56, C100-C103) positively. OpenEval provides detailed assessment of the mixed-methods approach and multi-level focus. Peer review implicitly supports this through praise for the broader implementation evaluation, noting it will 'evaluate efficacy and effectiveness in real-word context.'

Both evaluate the data governance and management structure (C51-C52, C79-C82) as appropriate. OpenEval explicitly praises the 'data on loan' model and security protocols. Peer review implicitly supports this by raising no concerns and noting the study's integration into existing screening activities.

Strong disagreement on modeling claims (C5-C8, C35, C96-C99, C123-C130). OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN due to crude assumptions and lack of sensitivity analysis. Peer review rates as UNSUPPORTED, strongly criticizing the comparison as 'misleading' and 'unnecessary to attack vaccination,' noting methodological flaws in comparing 20 screening cohorts to 5 vaccination cohorts.

Disagreement on study design clarity (C18-C21, C64, C104). OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED, finding design parameters 'straightforward' and 'internally consistent.' Peer review rates as UNCERTAIN, with one reviewer unable to locate enrollment numbers and timelines, indicating 'inadequate presentation of this critical information.'

Both evaluate the effectiveness phase and economic evaluation (C57-C58, C90-C95) positively. OpenEval finds the microsimulation and micro-costing approaches 'appropriate.' Peer review praises the 'inclusion of implementation evaluation' as 'an important milestone,' emphasizing that 'results of phase 2 are key to ensure future implementation.'

Both evaluate AI algorithm retraining (C83-C84) positively. OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN, acknowledging the approach is reasonable but performance 'remains to be demonstrated.' Peer review rates as SUPPORTED, explicitly praising the move to dedicated devices that 'overcomes challenges previously encountered' with mobile phone updates.

Both evaluate ScreenFire assay validation (C26-C27) positively. OpenEval finds validation data 'adequate for the study purpose' with performance comparable to reference methods. Peer review explicitly notes the triage 'builds on the authors' previously published work' as a strength, with no concerns raised about validation.

Both evaluate the blinded efficacy phase design (C33-C34) positively. OpenEval finds it 'appropriate for unbiased evaluation.' Peer review notes as a strength 'The separation of the study into two phases' with the efficacy phase evaluating AVE against biopsy outcomes.

Partial overlap on study objectives (C28, C32). OpenEval rates design as SUPPORTED with clearly stated hypothesis. Peer review rates as UNCERTAIN, criticizing lack of detailed statistical methods and power calculations, noting '"comparing" is not statistics.'

Disagreement on clinical protocol and biopsy procedures (C46-C49, C131). OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED, finding protocol 'well-designed with appropriate safety measures' and variation across sites 'appropriate.' Peer review rates as UNCERTAIN, identifying 'critical weakness' of potential ascertainment bias due to lack of specified biopsy protocol when aceto-white areas not identified, which 'may lead to an over-estimate of sensitivity.'

Both evaluate the PAVE approach combining HPV genotyping, AVE, and ScreenFire (C22, C24-C25, C29, C38-C39) positively. OpenEval rates clinical protocol as SUPPORTED and well-designed. Peer review affirms as 'probably the best available combination today' and notes it 'combined three key innovations,' with editor confirming it will 'generate convincing evidence.'

Partial overlap on timeline (C36-C37). OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED, noting timeline is appropriately stated as expectation. Peer review rates broader design elements as UNCERTAIN, with reviewer unable to locate timeline information, suggesting presentation issues.

Minimal overlap on reproducibility assessment (C88). OpenEval rates plans for measuring AUC variability as SUPPORTED and 'sound approaches.' Peer review criticizes lack of statistical methods and power calculations in the broader study design.
